Body Positivity

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We share the inspirational stories of women who have challenged societal norms of physical appearance and love the bodies they’re in.

Unique Selling Point:
Societal expectations of the perfect body being slim and trim have been the norm for the last hundred years creating barriers for plus size people who feel they don’t fit in. But in the last decade the body positivity movement has changed the landscape to embrace acceptance of all bodies no matter what shape, size or ethnicity. Body positivity is about working towards a world where everyone can live in their bodies as they please while receiving the same respect, representation, and opportunities as everyone else.

Summary:
We share the uplifting stories of women who have, despite discrimination based on their size, come out stronger. Through their journey of self-discovery they have turned their lives around and learnt to embrace their differentness. By celebrating their female form publicly on social media they have attracted many followers and served as an inspiration to others.
We go on a journey with four different women of diverse backgrounds and talents who each in their own right have become a body ambassador with a holistic approach to self -love and self-care.
We look at the role of healthy living and talk to a dietician who encourages natural weight loss through intuitive eating - an anti-diet approach to eating that focuses on people’s relationship and connectivity to their body’s natural cues for hunger and fullness.


Further information:
Meg Ringdal is an outspoken thirty something mom, blogger, and ambassador for several fashion and beauty brands who have learnt to take no prisoners. Once on a fashion shoot she told guests “No one should change their body to fit clothes that were not even created for them.”
Ringdal had a tough time at school as the ‘big girl’. “I was ashamed of my body. I started developing when I was only 9 years old”. She remembers attracting unwanted attention from men due to her curviness and this led to punishing herself. She over exercised, binged, purged, anything to get her weight down. This continued well in her teens. “I found it hard to have freedom in how I dress. I used to cover up my body to blend in”, she says.
Then seven years ago Ringdal started a low key blog called “Mind The Curve” which later became her instagram account where she started pushing the boundaries with her frank posts on body politics, diet and the fallacies that exist for large bodied people. She received heartbreaking messages of people in similar positions who could associate with her which helped to build her confidence. Today she is a successful career woman running her own business as a Body Stress Release Practitioner in Cape Town.

Boitumelo Ratmetsi is a vitiligo model from Soweto where she lives with her parents. She has a son and works as a freelance content writer and storyteller in addition to her modeling work. As a ‘spotted beauty’ she gives diversity by giving a voice to the silenced or ignored and misunderstood. “Imagine being black and divergent to ordinary pigmentation. To add on to that, imagine being a big girl that is considered to be disfigured and too large to be dressed beautifully. You basically become a plaque in society that no one wants to be associated with. Your opinion is a sideline and your character is not considered”, she says.
Rametsi has learnt to accept herself as a multidimensional human being who advocates variation and a non judgemental. As a Body Positive philanthropist she has a strong following on Instagram who has embraced her differentness and is challenging society to do the same.

Shirmeez Samaai is a post grad student from The University of the Western Cape doing her master’s in Body Positivity. She is in her late twenties and lives with her parents in Mitchells Plain where she gives dance classes every Friday. Her passion for dance started at an early age when she wanted to do ballet but was classed ‘too fat’. Hurtful comments about her big size continued throughout her school career. “At university I used to hide away in my room and never socialised. I felt out of place. It was only in my second year that I took the plunge and stopped covering my body all the time,” she says. Excelling in her academic career eventually gave Samaai confidence and through her dancing she found a freedom of expression. My classes are for all sizes, ages and shapes, and I use my dancing to show people they too can enjoy the freedom I experience in movement,” says Samaai.
Alex Beazley is a body positive model and content writer from Johannesburg. She is a tall and big girl who had to learn to “grow a thick skin”, she says. “My dad used to make remarks at the dinner table when I was asking for seconds, which stuck with me my whole life. Or he would joke about my cellulite as cottage cheese damage. It was really hurtful,” says Beazley.
But Beazley learnt to take the punches and today she is a confident woman and a body positive blogger and influencer. “Self love doesn’t just happen after posting one picture of yourself in your underwear. It happens when you are constantly striving to be your most authentic self,” she quoted on her instagram.
Gayle Landau is a dietician from Parktown in Johannesburg who has a special interest in intuitive eating which encourages natural weight loss. “Essentially it is the opposite of traditional diet. It doesn’t impose guidelines about what to avoid and what or when to eat,” says Landay. Landau will discuss the role of eating habits and the holistic approach to mind body connection.
Treatment: We will sketch the landscape of each of our case studies in their different surroundings to emphasise their visual and inner space. Although there are four case studies, each one is different and this will provide the contrast in the story. Images of the journeys to self discovery will be depicted through images of their past in contrast to the present. Modeling images will be made available courtesy of some of the brands and photographers.

Press Release:


L I F E S T Y L E



Perfectly Flawed

In a world obsessed with health and diet, exercise and the perfect shape, a small but growing number of people are kicking back against the notion of bodily perfection and embracing the idea of physical and mental health at any weight. Carte Blanche meets influencers in the body positivity movement for a fresh take on what it means to feel confident.

Producer: Annalise Lubbe | Researcher: Tony Beamish | Presenter: Bongani Bingwa

Watch the trailer

Script:


Script: Body Positivity
Duration: 8 minutes
Date: 1 February 2021

Meg Ringdal: Body Positive Influencer: As a very little girl I did ballet classes, as many little girls do and I was always felt very disheartened no matter how hard I tried, I always got put in the back behind everybody else.

Alex Beazley: Body Positive Influencer: I remember little things like my family members would encourage us always to be active, and you never really knew what the route cause of being active was, but it was to be thin!

Shirmeez Samaai: Body Positive Influencer: They were like, you can’t dance, you are too fat, and they used to ridicule me, they laughed at me. I thought that oh my goodness I cannot dance because I am fat!

V/O Society has always held up an ideal - but unrealistic - body type that we tend to strive for. We feel pressured to conform to that elusive but ‘acceptable weight’. For many it results in a damaged self-image and low self esteem.

Link: Small, medium, large, extra large: are you really happy with your size? Diet and exercise are multi-billion rand industries as many people spend fortunes to look just the right way, and not because they are unhealthy, but because of societal pressure.

V/O From early childhood, insensitive comments about weight come from those closest, and most difficult to ignore.

Alex Beazley: Our parents always want to help us, but little things like comments at Christmas for example, when we are dishing up seconds: “oh you are having another plate, are you?” Or “oh..”

Bongani Bingwa: Are you sure?

Ales Beazley: “Isn’t that a bit much?” Are you sure? Oh you are also having desert!

V/O As a young adult, no matter how hard she tried, Beazley’s weight never dropped to the ‘ideal body’ size portrayed as the norm. Her ‘self realisation’ came not too long ago.

Bongani Bingwa: What was your aha moment when you realised that actually “I am ok the way I am”?

Alex Beazley: I was on a beach in Cape Town and I put on a whole bunch of weight and I had the option to choose a full swimming costume, or I had the option to wear a bikini. And I put on that bikini and it was the first time I really got to like breath.

Bongani Bingwa. It was liberating wasn’t it?

Alex Beazley: Extremely!

Up music

V/O Social media has become the frontier for body-positive expression and a platform for Beazly to send out her encouraging messages of fashion tips for plus-size women.

Up sound - Beazley doing a youtube video on bikini: “So we have a beautiful peachy little colour......I feel super confident in this bikini.”

Link: For all its ugliness, social media has become a safe space for the Body Positive community to share stories of inspiration particularly for those who are still battling insecurities for being different.

Meg Ringdal: Body Positivity is a journey, it is definitely not a switch that gets flicked. But it is something that happened slowly over many years actually.

V/O For Meg Ringdal, a thirty-something mom, blogger, and ambassador for several fashion brands, the journey has been a roller coaster ride with weight issues and low self esteem before finding her self-worth.

Meg Ringdal: I sort of joked this journey started with “I am just the fat girl who liked dresses and wanted to find some options that fitted me”. And as I delved deeper and deeper into this world I learnt that there is so much more to it and that the problem is not with me at all you know, but society and the system around us.

Up music

V/O Ringdal is an influencer of the Body Positivity community. She remembers her first modeling experience.

Meg Ringdal: I felt rebellious but empowered and to send the message to other women that actually this is what my body looks like; this is a normal healthy body and there is nothing wrong with your body either.

V/O Body Positivity also embraces ‘uniqueness’. Boitumelo Rametsi, a visual storyteller from Soweto and mother of Samu, accepted her size but struggled with spots appearing on her body. The condition - vitiligo or loss of pigment-producing cells - got worse at university so she tried to hide it with make-up.

Boitumelo Rametsi: Body Positive influencer: I just felt I was caged in my own body having this make-up on. I had to decide that it is about me and how I feel in my body and what I think about myself matters more.

V/O When Rametsi started posting about her condition on Instagram she got mixed messages, some very negative.

Boitumelo Rametsi: The cyberbullying came on social media with people’s comments like: “ah you look like you have semen on your face”.

Bongani Bingwa: How did you deal with nasty comments?

Boitumelo Rametsi: People’s opinions really don't matter to me. I just grew up that way.

Up music

V/O And that is what her Instagram followers see - Rametsi through her own camera lens.

Boitumelo Rametsi: So that process in itself has led me to accepting my body changes as well as my identity which is perceived in obviously many different ways.

Bongani Bingwa: One of the things you are strong about is being black, being big but also having divergent pigmentation. What does that mean?

Boitumelo Rametsi: It just means more uniqueness, more individuality for me and a better identification of self.

V/O Expressing her individuality was difficult for 26-year-old Shirmeez Samaai, a dance instructor from Mitchells Plain. It took years to shake off the hurtful comments from school mates.

Shirmeez Samaai: Ever since that experience of being bullied I stopped dancing in public and it was more of a private thing where I would lock my room door and I would dance.

Up sound: “Jiggle all that holiday food we all eat.”

V/O But as Samaai grew more confident about her abilities as a dancer, she became an instructor at a gym. She has now even registered for a Master’s degree at the University of the Western Cape on society’s portrayal of the ‘ideal healthy body’ in magazines.

Shirmeez Samaai: Traditionally the slim woman is equated with being healthy as well as beautiful, so what does that mean for other bodies? I want people to know that you can be healthy at any size as long as you are eating well, you are exercising and you are practicing self-love every day.

V/O The Body Positivity community strongly emphsises exercise and healthy eating. Dietitian Gayle Landau has helped develop a mindful or intuitive eating approach and counsels clients to restore a healthy relationship with food.

Gayle Landau: Dietitian: I chose to do a self-study into Intuitive Eating when I became a bit disillusioned with the weight loss approach which was rooted in a belief that you can only be healthy if you are a certain weight.

Bongani Bingwa: Or a certain size.

Gayle Landau: Or a certain size.

Bongani Bingwa: But aren’t you ‘what you eat’?

Gayle Landau: You are what you eat but not in terms of your size so with Intuitive Eating we can attain health goals by making nutritious choices that feel good for the body.

Bongani Bingwa: To be clear, you are not saying obesity is ok?

Gayle Landau: I am saying that we need to move away from the stigma that makes the assumption that someone who is obese is unhealthy. If you look at body mass index which is where we get the term obesity, because of a classification, metabolically, in other words when these patients have blood tests, they don't necessarily have abnormal blood sugars they don't necessarily all have high cholesterol.

Bongani: So we should do away with even the word obesity?

Gayle: Ideally. We need to move away from the stigmatising type of words and understand that it is a medical condition that requires a multidisciplinary broad approach.

V/O Ringdal firmly believes in Intuitive Eating - listening to her body’s own hunger cues.

Meg Ringdal: Intuitive eating is wonderful for getting back in touch with your body and what your body’s needs are.

V/O Perhaps the biggest drive of the Body Positivity movement has been acceptance by society of health at every size and to remove the stigma attached to those who are different.

Alex Beazley: It is 100% ok to not be perfect. Any kind of thing you think is wrong with you is not. It is the way you were designed, the way you were built.

_____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Promo 1: For some people weight has always been a struggle. But four extraordinary women are finding ways to make peace with the way they look.

Promo 2: On YouTube and Instagram meet the Body Positivity movement. Every ‘body’ is acceptable no matter what size, shape or colour.

Promo 3: We share the stories of four Body Positive influencers who are challenging society’s norms of what the ideal weight should be: they love their bodies.

Boitumelo Rametsi: People’s opinions really don't matter to me. I just grew up that way. Up music V/O And that is what her Instagram followers see - Rametsi through her own camera lens. Boitumelo Rametsi: So that process in itself has led me to accepting my body changes as well as my identity which is perceived in obviously many different ways. Bongani Bingwa: One of the things you are strong about is being black, being big but also having divergent pigmentation. What does that mean? Boitumelo Rametsi: It just means more uniqueness, more individuality for me and a better identification of self. V/O Expressing her individuality was difficult for 26-year-old Shirmeez Samaai, a dance instructor from Mitchells Plain. It took years to shake off the hurtful comments from school mates. Shirmeez Samaai: Ever since that experience of being bullied I stopped dancing in public and it was more of a private thing where I would lock my room door and I would dance. Up sound: “Jiggle all that holiday food we all eat.” V/O But as Samaai grew more confident about her abilities as a dancer, she became an instructor at a gym. She has now even registered for a Master’s degree at the University of the Western Cape on society’s portrayal of the ‘ideal healthy body’ in magazines. Shirmeez Samaai: Traditionally the slim woman is equated with being healthy as well as beautiful, so what does that mean for other bodies? I want people to know that you can be healthy at any size as long as you are eating well, you are exercising and you are practicing self-love every day. V/O The Body Positivity community strongly emphsises exercise and healthy eating. Dietitian Gayle Landau has helped develop a mindful or intuitive eating approach and counsels clients to restore a healthy relationship with food. Gayle Landau: Dietitian: I chose to do a self-study into Intuitive Eating when I became a bit disillusioned with the weight loss approach which was rooted in a belief that you can only be healthy if you are a certain weight. Bongani Bingwa: Or a certain size. Gayle Landau: Or a certain size. Bongani Bingwa: But aren’t you ‘what you eat’? Gayle Landau: You are what you eat but not in terms of your size so with Intuitive Eating we can attain health goals by making nutritious choices that feel good for the body. Bongani Bingwa: To be clear, you are not saying obesity is ok? Gayle Landau: I am saying that we need to move away from the stigma that makes the assumption that someone who is obese is unhealthy. If you look at body mass index which is where we get the term obesity, because of a classification, metabolically, in other words when these patients have blood tests, they don't necessarily have abnormal blood sugars they don't necessarily all have high cholesterol. Bongani: So we should do away with even the word obesity? Gayle: Ideally. We need to move away from the stigmatising type of words and understand that it is a medical condition that requires a multidisciplinary broad approach. V/O Ringdal firmly believes in Intuitive Eating - listening to her body’s own hunger cues. Meg Ringdal: Intuitive eating is wonderful for getting back in touch with your body and what your body’s needs are. V/O Perhaps the biggest drive of the Body Positivity movement has been acceptance by society of health at every size and to remove the stigma attached to those who are different. Alex Beazley: It is 100% ok to not be perfect. Any kind of thing you think is wrong with you is not. It is the way you were designed, the way you were built. _____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promo 1: For some people weight has always been a struggle. But four extraordinary women are finding ways to make peace with the way they look. Promo 2: On YouTube and Instagram meet the Body Positivity movement. Every ‘body’ is acceptable no matter what size, shape or colour. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We share the inspirational stories of women who have challenged societal norms of physical appearance and love the bodies they’re in.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Societal expectations of the perfect body being slim and trim have been the norm for the last hundred years creating barriers for plus size people who feel they don’t fit in. But in the last decade the body positivity movement has changed the landscape to embrace acceptance of all bodies no matter what shape, size or ethnicity. Body positivity is about working towards a world where everyone can live in their bodies as they please while receiving the same respect, representation, and opportunities as everyone else.
metadata.Summary: We share the uplifting stories of women who have, despite discrimination based on their size, come out stronger. Through their journey of self-discovery they have turned their lives around and learnt to embrace their differentness. By celebrating their female form publicly on social media they have attracted many followers and served as an inspiration to others. We go on a journey with four different women of diverse backgrounds and talents who each in their own right have become a body ambassador with a holistic approach to self -love and self-care. We look at the role of healthy living and talk to a dietician who encourages natural weight loss through intuitive eating - an anti-diet approach to eating that focuses on people’s relationship and connectivity to their body’s natural cues for hunger and fullness.
metadata.Further information: Meg Ringdal is an outspoken thirty something mom, blogger, and ambassador for several fashion and beauty brands who have learnt to take no prisoners. Once on a fashion shoot she told guests “No one should change their body to fit clothes that were not even created for them.” Ringdal had a tough time at school as the ‘big girl’. “I was ashamed of my body. I started developing when I was only 9 years old”. She remembers attracting unwanted attention from men due to her curviness and this led to punishing herself. She over exercised, binged, purged, anything to get her weight down. This continued well in her teens. “I found it hard to have freedom in how I dress. I used to cover up my body to blend in”, she says. Then seven years ago Ringdal started a low key blog called “Mind The Curve” which later became her instagram account where she started pushing the boundaries with her frank posts on body politics, diet and the fallacies that exist for large bodied people. She received heartbreaking messages of people in similar positions who could associate with her which helped to build her confidence. Today she is a successful career woman running her own business as a Body Stress Release Practitioner in Cape Town. Boitumelo Ratmetsi is a vitiligo model from Soweto where she lives with her parents. She has a son and works as a freelance content writer and storyteller in addition to her modeling work. As a ‘spotted beauty’ she gives diversity by giving a voice to the silenced or ignored and misunderstood. “Imagine being black and divergent to ordinary pigmentation. To add on to that, imagine being a big girl that is considered to be disfigured and too large to be dressed beautifully. You basically become a plaque in society that no one wants to be associated with. Your opinion is a sideline and your character is not considered”, she says. Rametsi has learnt to accept herself as a multidimensional human being who advocates variation and a non judgemental. As a Body Positive philanthropist she has a strong following on Instagram who has embraced her differentness and is challenging society to do the same. Shirmeez Samaai is a post grad student from The University of the Western Cape doing her master’s in Body Positivity. She is in her late twenties and lives with her parents in Mitchells Plain where she gives dance classes every Friday. Her passion for dance started at an early age when she wanted to do ballet but was classed ‘too fat’. Hurtful comments about her big size continued throughout her school career. “At university I used to hide away in my room and never socialised. I felt out of place. It was only in my second year that I took the plunge and stopped covering my body all the time,” she says. Excelling in her academic career eventually gave Samaai confidence and through her dancing she found a freedom of expression. My classes are for all sizes, ages and shapes, and I use my dancing to show people they too can enjoy the freedom I experience in movement,” says Samaai. Alex Beazley is a body positive model and content writer from Johannesburg. She is a tall and big girl who had to learn to “grow a thick skin”, she says. “My dad used to make remarks at the dinner table when I was asking for seconds, which stuck with me my whole life. Or he would joke about my cellulite as cottage cheese damage. It was really hurtful,” says Beazley. But Beazley learnt to take the punches and today she is a confident woman and a body positive blogger and influencer. “Self love doesn’t just happen after posting one picture of yourself in your underwear. It happens when you are constantly striving to be your most authentic self,” she quoted on her instagram. Gayle Landau is a dietician from Parktown in Johannesburg who has a special interest in intuitive eating which encourages natural weight loss. “Essentially it is the opposite of traditional diet. It doesn’t impose guidelines about what to avoid and what or when to eat,” says Landay. Landau will discuss the role of eating habits and the holistic approach to mind body connection. Treatment: We will sketch the landscape of each of our case studies in their different surroundings to emphasise their visual and inner space. Although there are four case studies, each one is different and this will provide the contrast in the story. Images of the journeys to self discovery will be depicted through images of their past in contrast to the present. Modeling images will be made available courtesy of some of the brands and photographers.
